findings.title: Downsize reads and writes the same tempfile path
findings.body: OptimizedImage.downsize is invoked with tempfile.path as both the source and the destination. The convert command built by downsize_instructions opens the output path for writing before it finishes reading the input, so when those paths are identical ImageMagick truncates the upload and the result is an empty or corrupt image. Versions that special-case this by writing a temporary file and renaming it over the destination leave the already-open Ruby Tempfile descriptor on the old inode while the path points at the new file. Upload.create_for on line 72 is then given that Tempfile object and tempfile.size, so the bytes stored, the SHA1 (if taken from the path), and the recorded filesize can disagree, and the saved upload is not the image the user sent.

findings.title: Downsize path has no image extension, so encoding and GIF detection fail
findings.body: create_upload passes tempfile.path straight through and never copies the bytes to a file ending in the original filename's extension. Multipart uploads use Rack's Tempfile (Tempfile.new("RackMultipart")), which has no .jpg/.png/.gif suffix, and the URL branch asks FileHelper.download for a "discourse-upload-#{type}" prefix that also does not include filename's extension. ImageMagick chooses the output encoder from the destination extension, so this convert fails with no encode delegate or writes a payload that is not the format implied by original_filename. optimize only takes the gifsicle path when the source path ends in .gif, so the allow_animation flag passed here does not apply and a GIF is sent through convert's [0] selector, which keeps only the first frame.

findings.title: Failed downsize is ignored and the file is still uploaded
findings.body: The loop discards the false return from OptimizedImage.downsize. convert_with returns false when convert, gifsicle, or ImageOptim fails, but the only exit condition is tempfile.size. A convert that truncates the file makes size 0, the while condition ends, and the empty file is treated as small enough and passed to Upload.create_for. If conversion fails without shrinking the file, the loop retries up to five times and then still calls create_for even though the image is larger than SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb. downsize_instructions also sets no JPEG -quality, so a re-encode at ImageMagick's default quality can grow the file across attempts. The feature does not enforce the size limit and can persist a truncated or oversized upload.

findings.title: No maximum size before repeated ImageMagick conversion
findings.body: The new loop runs for every image larger than SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb and never rejects files above the 10MB ceiling added on the client and in the URL downloader. Multipart bodies are not size-capped in create_upload before this work, and the client check is bypassable by a direct POST or API call. Each attempt shells out to convert or gifsicle and then ImageOptim. Any logged-in user can submit a very large image, or a small decompression bomb whose name looks like an image, and force up to five full decodes on a defer thread or, for synchronous API uploads, on a web worker, exhausting CPU and memory before Upload.create_for can apply a filesize error.

findings.title: Second downsize definition overwrites the width/height API
findings.body: Ruby does not overload by arity, so def self.downsize(from, to, dimensions, opts={}) on line 149 replaces def self.downsize(from, to, max_width, max_height, opts={}) on line 145 at load time and emits a method-redefined warning. The width/height implementation is dead. This class previously exposed downsize(from, to, max_width, max_height, opts). Callers that still pass width, height, and an options hash now raise ArgumentError (5 arguments for a method that accepts at most 4). Callers that pass width and height only bind height to opts, and optimize then raises TypeError on opts[:allow_animation] because an Integer does not accept a Symbol index. The new uploads-controller call only works because it matches the surviving definition; definition order, not an overload, is what makes "80%" work.

findings.title: Client size check hardcodes 10MB for every upload type
findings.body: validateUploadedFile used to compare against Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb'], so images and attachments honored separate admin limits. It now always uses 10 * 1024 KB. Attachments larger than max_attachment_size_kb but under 10MB pass the client and are not downsized by the new server loop; attachments that the admin allowed above 10MB are rejected. Images are capped at 10MB even if max_image_size_kb is higher, and a max_image_size_kb of 0 (which skips server downsize because the new guard requires > 0) still hits this fixed client cap. The 413 handler on line 246 repeats the same constant, so the user-facing file_too_large message always claims the maximum is 10240 KB even when the proxy or the site setting rejected the file for a different limit.

findings.title: URL fetch limit ignores per-type size settings
findings.body: FileHelper.download used to stop at SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb.kilobytes. It now always allows 10.megabytes, and this runs before the code knows whether the URL is an image. Non-image API uploads are not passed through the new downsize loop, so a remote attachment or other non-image is fetched up to 10MB even when max_attachment_size_kb or max_image_size_kb is lower. That raises the amount of data an API client can pull into the temp directory and no longer matches the configured per-type limit.

findings.title: 80% geometry and thumbnail setting do not correctly downsize GIFs
findings.body: The third argument is the ImageMagick percentage "80%", but when the path ends in .gif and allow_animation is true, optimize uses gifsicle --resize-fit with that string. --resize-fit is built for a pixel box such as 800x600 (resize_instructions_animated), not an ImageMagick percentage, so the animated shrink fails and, because the return value is ignored, the GIF is left over the size limit. allow_animation is also bound to SiteSetting.allow_animated_thumbnails. When that thumbnail setting is off, the canonical upload goes through convert's [0] frame selector and the stored GIF silently loses every frame but the first, even though the setting is not supposed to rewrite originals.

findings.title: No tests cover automatic downsize or the new size ceiling
findings.body: The new behavior — image-only shrinking, a five-attempt 80% loop, what happens when convert fails or the file stays over max_image_size_kb, non-image uploads still bound by their own site setting, and the OptimizedImage.downsize signature change — has no tests in this pull request. A regression that stores a truncated tempfile or rejects a previously allowed attachment would not be caught.
